title: Does a Heat Pump Ever Pay for Itself?

sentences.text: A common pitch for a heat pump ends the same way: it pays for itself.

sentences.text: Over the life of the equipment and without any subsidy, compared with replacing the old equipment like for like when it wears out, 59 percent came out ahead if every home picked its single best option.

But no real buyer gets to pick with perfect hindsight, and no single heat pump did that well: the cheapest, minimum-efficiency units came out ahead in 55 percent of homes, and the premium cold-climate units in only 21 percent, because their higher price ate the extra savings.

3.5. Heat pump adoption rates vary by electric grid region, climate, housing characteristics, and
baseline heating fuel Perhaps the most important indicator of whether a home’s adoption of a heat
pump produces a benefit is its current heating fuel. Switching a home’s heating fuel from natural
gas to heat pumps rarely produces a benefit, especially in cold climates where there are almost no
houses where such a switch makes sense. If there is opportunity for beneficially replacing natural
gas heaters with heat pumps, it will be in mediumefficiency houses (1970–1989 vintage) in hot or
mild climates.

sentences.text: On oil, the models disagree.

The national lab model, counting the cost of the equipment, found a basic heat pump came out ahead over its life for most homes heated with fuel oil; the second model found a switch from oil "usually causes the homeowner a private economic loss", in part because nearly 65 percent of oil-heated houses are in cold climates.

sentences.text: A Minnesota study priced a cold-climate heat pump with a propane furnace as backup at $9,450 installed, using a national cost database.

Installed while the old furnace and air conditioner still worked, its simple payback came to 14.5 years against an older furnace and 28.8 years against an efficient condensing one, longer than the 18 years the study expects the equipment to last.
Installed when both had failed and needed replacing anyway, the extra cost fell to just $370, and the payback to between 0.6 and 1.1 years.

sentences.text: A model of gas-heated homes in Chicago, Providence, Houston and Oakland, at the energy prices it used, found the same pattern.
Switching paid off for gas customers who "would otherwise need to replace both a furnace and air conditioner simultaneously".

Otherwise, existing gas homes that switched both heating and water heating to electric either paid more for energy, in colder Chicago and Providence, or saved too little to make up the extra cost, in Houston and Oakland.

sentences.text: Put the pieces together and a pattern appears.
If you are leaving propane or electric resistance heat, a heat pump usually pays.

Buying when the old equipment is due for replacement is the case the national figures already describe; in the Minnesota example, with a propane furnace as backup, replacing a failed furnace and air conditioner together cut the payback from decades to about a year.
And if you are tearing out a working gas furnace, the models mostly say it will not pay back on energy savings alone.
